chapters.title: Chapter 1: How Income Tax in India Is Structured

lessons.title: Tax Year, Residential Status and Who the Slabs Apply To

children.text: Before you can apply a single slab, three questions need answers. Which 12 months of income are we taxing? Is this taxpayer the kind of person the slabs are designed for? And how much of their worldwide income does India get to tax at all? Get any of these wrong and a perfectly correct slab calculation is applied to the wrong number.
Question 1: Which Year? The Tax Year

markDefs.definition: The 12-month period from 1 April to 31 March in which income is earned and taxed. Introduced by the Income-tax Act, 2025 in place of the separate previous year and assessment year.

children.text: For decades, Indian taxpayers juggled two labels. Income was earned in the "previous year" (the financial year) and assessed in the following "assessment year". Salary earned between April 2025 and March 2026 belonged to FY 2025-26 but was reported for AY 2026-27, a mismatch that confused almost every first-time filer. The Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026, replaces both with a single
under section 3 (sections 2(9) and 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1961). The year you earn in is the year you are taxed for.

columns.label: Income-tax Act, 1961
points: Income earned in the "previous year", also called the financial year (FY)
Assessed in the "assessment year" (AY) that follows
Income of April 2025 to March 2026 = FY 2025-26 = AY 2026-27
Still applies to income earned up to 31 March 2026

columns.label: Income-tax Act, 2025
points: Income of April 2026 to March 2027 = tax year 2026-27
Applies to income earned from 1 April 2026 onwards

body.text: The switch is not retroactive. The return you filed around July 2026 was for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27) under the 1961 Act. Tax year 2026-27 is the first year under the 2025 Act, and its return is filed in 2027. You will see both sets of labels on the income tax portal and in Form 26AS and AIS for some time.

body.title: The Life of Tax Year 2026-27 for a Salaried Taxpayer

events.title: Tax Year Begins
events.description: Every rupee of salary, interest and gains from today is counted in tax year 2026-27. Declare your regime choice to your employer so TDS is deducted correctly.

events.title: Advance Tax Instalments
events.description: Relevant if you have significant income beyond salary, such as capital gains, rent or freelance fees, on which TDS does not cover your full tax.

events.title: Final Advance Tax Instalment
events.description: The last date to pay the full estimated tax for the year without attracting interest for deferment.

events.title: Tax Year Ends
events.description: The slab calculation for the year is based on total income earned up to this date.

events.title: Usual Return Due Date
events.description: The normal due date for salaried individuals and others whose accounts do not need an audit, unless extended by the CBDT.

body.title: Tax Year Dates
body.textWithBlank: Tax year 2026-27 starts on 1 April 2026 and ends on ___.
body.explanation: A tax year always runs 1 April to 31 March. The one exception is a newly set up business or a new source of income, where the first tax year runs from the date of set-up to the following 31 March.

children.text: Question 2: Who? The Taxpayers That Use Slabs

Slabs are built for people, not corporations. Individuals and a handful of person-like entities use them. Businesses organised as firms, LLPs and companies pay flat rates on every rupee of profit instead.

cells: A salaried employee at Infosys, a freelance designer, a retired bank officer
Yes, same slabs as an individual
A family HUF that owns inherited rental property in Jaipur
Association of Persons (AOP) or Body of Individuals (BOI)
A group of friends jointly owning and letting out a shop
A CA firm or a family trading partnership
No, flat rates such as 22% under the concessional option
A private limited startup or a listed company like Tata Motors

body.label: Every Person Gets Their Own Slabs
body.value: India has no joint filing for couples
body.context: Husband and wife are separate taxpayers, each with their own 4 lakh exemption limit and their own slabs. A family with two earners pays far less than it would if their incomes were added together.

children.text: Take Aditya and Neha, a couple in Hyderabad, both under the new regime. Aditya's taxable income is ₹20,00,000 and Neha's is ₹8,00,000. Taxed separately, Aditya's slab tax is ₹2,00,000 (₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + ₹60,000 + ₹80,000). Neha's slab tax is ₹20,000, which the rebate you will meet in Chapter 3 reduces to zero. If India instead taxed their combined ₹28,00,000 as one income, the slab tax would be ₹4,20,000.

stats.label: Neha's Final Tax
stats.context: ₹20,000 slab tax, removed by the rebate

body.text: Separate taxation does not mean you can freely shift income to a lower-earning spouse. If Aditya gifts ₹10 lakh to Neha and she puts it in an FD, the clubbing rules add that FD interest back to Aditya's income. Splitting income across family members only works when the income genuinely belongs to each person.

children.text: Where Age Matters, and Where It Does Not

The new regime has one slab table for every individual, whether 25 or 85. The old regime gives resident senior citizens a higher exemption limit. You will work through the full old regime table in Chapter 2. For now, note that age only changes the zero-tax band, and only for residents.

body.caption: Nil-Tax Band by Age and Residential Status

cells: Resident super senior citizen, 80 and above

children.text: Question 3: How Much Income? Residential Status

markDefs.definition: Your status for Indian tax purposes in a given tax year, based on the number of days you are physically in India. It decides whether India taxes your worldwide income or only your Indian income. It has nothing to do with citizenship.

children.text: is worked out afresh every tax year under section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 6 of the 1961 Act). It depends on days spent in India, not on your passport. An Indian citizen working in Dubai can be a non-resident, and a foreign national posted to Bengaluru can be a resident.

body.caption: The Basic Residence Tests for an Individual

cells: In India for 182 days or more during the tax year
In India for 60 days or more in the tax year AND 365 days or more in the 4 preceding tax years

body.text: The 60-day limb is relaxed for Indian citizens in two situations. An Indian citizen who leaves India for employment abroad during the year, and an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin who lives abroad and visits India, have the 60 days replaced by 182 days. For visitors whose Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh, it is replaced by 120 days instead. This stops NRIs from becoming residents simply by spending a couple of months at home.

children.text: A resident is then further classified as either Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) or Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR). An individual is RNOR if they were a non-resident in 9 of the 10 preceding tax years, or spent 729 days or less in India across the 7 preceding tax years. Returning NRIs typically enjoy RNOR status for their first two or three years back.

body.caption: What Residential Status Decides: Which Income Enters the Slabs

cells: Salary for work done in India
Interest on an SBI or HDFC Bank FD
Rent from a flat in Pune
Salary for work done in Singapore, received there
Dividends from US shares held abroad
Profits of a foreign business controlled from India

body.text: Non-residents use the same new regime slabs as residents, but they lose two things. The rebate that makes income up to 12 lakh tax-free is available only to resident individuals. And under the old regime, the higher senior citizen exemption limits apply only to residents.

body.title: Work Out Your Status for Any Tax Year
steps: Count your days physically present in India between 1 April and 31 March, using your passport stamps or travel history
If the count is 182 or more, you are a resident. Skip to the RNOR check
If it is between 60 and 181, check whether you left India for employment abroad or are an Indian citizen or PIO visiting India. If so, apply the 182-day or 120-day version of the test instead
Otherwise, add up your days in India across the 4 preceding tax years. 365 or more makes you a resident
If resident, check the RNOR conditions: non-resident in 9 of the last 10 years, or 729 days or less in India over the last 7 years
Use the result to list which income enters your slab calculation, then check whether you qualify for the rebate

body.title: Meera Moves to Dubai
body.scenario: Meera, an Indian citizen, is a chartered accountant in Mumbai. She leaves India on 20 June 2026 to take up a job in Dubai and does not return during tax year 2026-27. She was in India every day of the previous four years. Her Indian income for the year is ₹3,20,000 of April to June salary and ₹60,000 of FD interest. In Dubai she earns the equivalent of ₹40,00,000.
body.prompt: What is Meera's residential status for tax year 2026-27, and which of her income goes into the Indian slab calculation?
body.modelAnswer: Meera spends 81 days in India (30 in April, 31 in May, 20 in June). That is below 182, so the first test fails. Normally 81 days plus her long stay in the previous four years would make her a resident under the 60 + 365-day test. But because she is an Indian citizen leaving India for employment abroad, the 60 days is replaced by 182 days, which she also fails. She is a non-resident. Only her Indian income of ₹3,80,000 (salary for work done in India plus FD interest) is taxed in India. Her Dubai salary stays out of the slab calculation entirely. Her Indian income is below the 4 lakh exemption limit, so she has no slab tax, but she should still ensure her bank reclassifies her savings and FDs as NRO accounts.

body.title: Farhan's Home Visit
body.question: Farhan, an Indian citizen, has worked in Singapore for six years. In tax year 2026-27 he visits family in Lucknow for 75 days. He spent 500 days in India across the previous four years, and his Indian income is ₹4,00,000 of rent. What is his residential status?
options: Resident, because he meets the 60-day and 365-day conditions
Non-resident, because as a visiting citizen with Indian income up to ₹15 lakh his 60-day condition becomes 182 days
RNOR, because he spent more than 60 days in India
Resident, because every Indian citizen is resident for Indian tax
body.explanation: Farhan would pass the ordinary 60 + 365-day test. But the relaxation for visiting Indian citizens replaces 60 days with 182 days when Indian income is ₹15 lakh or less. At 75 days he fails it and is a non-resident. Citizenship alone never makes someone a resident.

body.title: Going deeper: the 120-day rule and deemed residents

children.text: Vikram, an Indian citizen working in the US, owns three flats in Bengaluru and has Indian income of ₹18,00,000. He visits India for 130 days and spent 400 days here over the previous four years. Because his Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh, his 60-day condition becomes 120 days rather than 182. At 130 days plus 400 days over four years, he is a resident. The law then automatically treats someone who is resident only through this 120-day route as RNOR, so India taxes his Indian income but not his US salary.

Separately, an Indian citizen with Indian income above ₹15 lakh who is not liable to tax in any other country because of domicile or residence is a deemed resident of India, again classified as RNOR. This targets citizens who live in zero-tax jurisdictions and would otherwise pay tax nowhere.

cards.definition: The 1 April to 31 March period in which income is earned and taxed, under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Replaces the previous year and assessment year.
Hindu Undivided Family. A separate taxpayer with its own PAN that uses the same slabs as an individual.
A resident taxed in India on worldwide income.
A resident, often a returning NRI, taxed mainly on Indian income and income from a business controlled or profession set up in India.
An individual who fails the residence tests for the year. Taxed only on income received, accruing or arising in India, and not eligible for the rebate.
Rules that add certain income of a spouse or minor child, such as returns on money you gifted them, to your own income.

points: From 1 April 2026, income is earned and taxed in a single "tax year"; income up to 31 March 2026 still follows the FY and AY labels of the 1961 Act
Individuals, HUFs, AOPs and BOIs use slabs; firms, LLPs and companies pay flat rates
Every individual is taxed separately, so spouses each get their own exemption limit and slabs, subject to clubbing rules
Age changes only the nil-tax band, only under the old regime and only for residents
Residential status depends on days in India, not citizenship, and decides whether worldwide or only Indian income enters the slabs
Non-residents use the same new regime slabs but cannot claim the rebate

body.text: This lesson simplifies the residence rules to their core tests. Day counting, the treatment of seafarers and the interaction with Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements can change the outcome in individual cases. It is for education only and is not tax advice. If your status is borderline, confirm it with a chartered accountant before filing.
